e:
The adjective is a learned borrowing from French mi-parti (literally “divided down the middle”), from Middle French mi-parti, from Old French mi-parti, an adjective use of the past participle of mi-partir (“to split in half”), from mi- (prefix meaning ‘half’) + partir (“to divide up”):
* Mi- is from Middle French mi (“middle”), from Old French mi, mie (“middle”), ultimately from Latin medius (“half; in the centre, midway between”, adjective) and medium (“centre, middle”, noun), and from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”, adjective). Compare medial.
* Partir is from Latin partīre, the present active infinitive of partiō (“to apportion, divide”), from pars (“part, portion”, noun) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go or pass through”) or *perh₂- (“to sell”)) + -iō (suffix forming fourth-conjugation verbs). Compare party (“divided”).
Though the term is mentioned beginning in the 17th century, actual use is apparently mostly recorded from the 19th century onwards (but see the 1610 quotation).
The noun is derived from the adjective.
q: They are all parted per pale, or (to vſe [Jean] Scohiers vvord) mi-partie, that is, parted longvviſe in the midſt, or perpendicularly parted, but yet ſeuerally affected in the partings […]
1610, E[dmund] B[olton], “Evstace”, in The Elements of Armories, London: […] George Eld, →OCLC, page 95:

The new German Imperial flag has just been decided upon, and is adopted already by Bavaria, Würtemberg, and Baden. It is mi-partie or, sable, gules, and argent, and has for supporters the two Indians armed with maces of the Prussian crest.
1871 March 1, “The German Empire”, in The Times, number 26,999, London: Francis Goodlake, →ISSN, →OCLC, page 8, column 2:
Almost all the indoor servants were given three ells of coloured shortcloth, together with three ells of striped cloth for their suits, which must have been, therefore, mi-parti.

1980, Stella Mary Newton, “Livery and the Dress of the Poor”, in Fashion in the Age of the Black Prince: A Study of the Years 1340–1365, Woodbridge, Suffolk: Boydell Press; Totowa, N.J.: Rowman & Litt
All the colors of the Universe radiate off the walls and floor of this room. The being here is dressed in a miparti …

e: From Glover's solmization, from Middle English mi (“third degree or note of Guido of Arezzo's hexachordal scales”), Italian mi in the solmization of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin mīra (“miracles; the miraculous”) in the lyrics of the scale-ascending hymn Ut queant laxis by Paulus Deacon.
